R1.4.response: You are right, and we thank you for pressing on it, because the asymmetry made the timing column uninterpretable. Writing the warning in capitals in the caption did not fix the problem; it only advertised it. Every timing figure in the revision has been re-measured. All models, including the deep baselines, are now trained and timed on the CPU of a single machine, under one measurement harness, with the same thread budget. The machine is specified in full in a new environment table: Intel Core i9-13900H, 14 cores and 20 threads, 2.60 GHz base clock, 47.6 GB of memory, Windows 11 Pro. The PyTorch build installed in the measurement environment carries no CUDA support, so no model in the comparison can be timed on a GPU even inadvertently. Re-measuring also exposed an unrelated artifact in the submitted timings that we would not otherwise have found. The Random Forest was being timed with parallel tree dispatch enabled while scoring one flow at a time, so the reported figure was dominated by thread-dispatch overhead rather than by inference, and it made the Random Forest look two orders of magnitude slower than it is. Forcing serial evaluation for single-flow latency removes the artifact, and the corrected figures are the ones now reported.
R1.4.action: Re-measured every timing figure on one CPU-only machine under a single harness, added a hardware and software environment table, removed the capitalized caveat from the table caption, and corrected a thread-dispatch artifact in the single-flow latency measurement.
R1.4.location: Sec. VI-C (Computing environment) and Table 5; the baseline comparison tables in Sec. VIII

R1.5.response: Done, and thank you for the suggestion; it improved the paper more than we expected. Every baseline is now reported CPU-only, and two comparisons are provided rather than one. The first runs every classical baseline on the full chronological split at the natural class imbalance, with no subsampling and no artificial balancing, which is the setting an operator actually faces. The second runs the deep baselines, a 1D-CNN, an LSTM, a Transformer encoder, a reconstruction autoencoder and a graph neural network, under a protocol matched across those models, again on the CPU. Both are measured with the same harness on the machine specified in Table 5, so latency and throughput are comparable across every row of every table in the paper. Where a baseline could not be run at full scale we say so explicitly and report the cap rather than quietly omitting the model: the linear support vector machine is fitted on a capped subsample of 300,000 flows because it did not converge in reasonable time on 2.5 million, and that cap is stated both in the table and in the text. The RBF support vector machine does not scale to the full partition at all, its kernel being quadratic in the sample count, so it is reported under the subsampled protocol only and its figure is given in the text of Sec. VIII-A rather than placed in a column measured on 1,077,238 flows.
R1.5.action: Added CPU-only results for every classical and deep baseline under two clearly separated protocols, with all timings produced by one harness on one machine, and stated every scale cap explicitly.
R1.5.location: Sec. VIII-A and Sec. VIII-B, with their tables; Table 5

R7.4.response: We agree, and we are grateful for the comment, because the evidence it produced is more informative than a simple confirmation would have been. The revision evaluates the detector on four further attack vectors from the same corpus, on a second capture day, and on two independent datasets, and it reports the failures alongside the successes. Within the capture, transfer to other reflection and amplification vectors is strong. Trained on SYN alone and tested zero-shot, the detector reaches macro F1 0.9692 on LDAP, 0.9566 on NetBIOS and 0.9896 on Portmap. Leave-one-vector-out training gives 0.9663, 0.9734 and 0.9709 on the same three vectors. Transfer in the other direction is weaker: training on LDAP, NetBIOS and Portmap and testing on SYN gives macro F1 0.6966 with a false-negative rate of 6.93 percent. Across capture days the picture is worse and we report it plainly. Trained on the 03-11 SYN partition and tested on the 01-12 SYN partition, macro F1 falls to 0.4995, although the false-negative rate remains 3.47 percent; the collapse is driven by the benign class, of which the 01-12 partition contains only 356 flows, and we say so rather than presenting the headline number without its cause. Across datasets the detector does not transfer at all. Zero-shot macro F1 is 0.6026 on InSDN and 0.2788 on CIC-IDS2017, the latter with a false-negative rate of 98.13 percent. The text states that this is a negative result, that a model trained on one corpus should not be deployed on another without retraining, and that the generalization claims of the submitted version were not supported. Every figure above carries a bootstrap confidence interval on the error rates.
R7.4.action: Added a cross-vector and cross-day evaluation covering four vectors and two capture days, and a cross-dataset evaluation on InSDN and CIC-IDS2017 under zero-shot, in-distribution and joint-training conditions, reporting the transfer failures explicitly and revising the generalization claims accordingly.
R7.4.location: Sec. VII-J (Transfer: other vectors, another day, another corpus) and Table 12, Sec. IX-D (Limitations and threats to validity)
